title: Fractions Basics
objectives: Understand fractions as parts of a whole
Add and subtract fractions with like and unlike denominators

introduction.context: Fractions represent the pinnacle of basic arithmetic, introducing parts of wholes and enabling precise measurements, ratios, and proportional thinking that underpin advanced mathematics like algebra and calculus. This chapter extends the operations from prior chapters: place value from Chapter 1 gives structure to decimal equivalents, addition/subtraction from Chapter 2 handles combining parts, multiplication from Chapter 3 scales fractions, and division from Chapter 4 forms their very definition (numerator divided by denominator).
introduction.connection: Fractions build directly on division from Chapter 4. A fraction like 3/4 means 3 ÷ 4, representing 3 parts out of 4 equal parts. The operations you learned in previous chapters extend naturally to fractions, with some important modifications for handling different denominators.

concepts.title: Understanding Fractions
concepts.content: Fractions begin with wholes divided into parts, intuitively like slicing a pie: one slice of four is 1/4. This part-whole relationship makes fractions essential for non-integer quantities. Formally, a fraction a/b represents a divided by b, where a is numerator, b denominator (b ≠ 0). Proper if |a| < |b|, improper otherwise (e.g., 5/3), mixed as whole + proper (1 2/3). Historically, Egyptians (2000 BCE) used eye of Horus for halves to 1/64. Babylonians had positional fractions. Greeks like Archimedes (200 BCE) approximated pi as fractions.
concepts.latex: \frac{a}{b} \text{ where } a \text{ is numerator, } b \text{ is denominator } (b \neq 0)

concepts.title: Equivalent Fractions and Simplifying
concepts.content: Equivalent fractions look different but equal value, like 1/2 = 2/4. Intuitively, halve a halved pie - same as quartering directly. Formally, a/b = c/d if a×d = b×c; generate by multiplying/dividing numerator/denominator by same k ≠ 0. History: Euclid proved equivalence via common measures. Arabs used for astronomy.

concepts.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions
concepts.content: Combining fractions requires common denominators, intuitively like aligning units: add 1/2 + 1/3 by sixths (3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6). Formally, a/b + c/d = (a×d + b×c)/(b×d); subtract similarly minus. History: Egyptians added unit fractions. Al-Khwarizmi used LCD.

concepts.title: Multiplying Fractions
concepts.content: Fraction multiplication scales parts: 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8, intuitively half of three-quarters. Formally, (a/b) × (c/d) = (a×c)/(b×d); simplify before/after. History: Babylonians multiplied fractions positionally. Greeks geometrically.

concepts.title: Dividing Fractions
concepts.content: Dividing fractions inverts: 1/2 ÷ 1/3 = 3/2, intuitively how many thirds in half? (1.5). Formally, (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c). History: Rhind Papyrus inverted. Modern rule from 1800s texts.

examples.problem: What fraction of the circle is shaded if 3 out of 8 equal parts are colored?
steps: Count the total number of equal parts: 8
Check: 3 parts out of 8 total parts
Find the least common denominator: LCM of 4 and 3 is 12

hints: Think about what fraction means the same as 1/2
1/2 means 1 part out of 2 equal parts
practice.explanation: 2/4 = 1/2 because both represent half of a whole. 2 out of 4 parts is the same as 1 out of 2 parts.
When denominators are the same, add the numerators: 2 + 1 = 3, so 2/5 + 1/5 = 3/5
To multiply fractions: (1 × 2)/(4 × 3) = 2/12, which can be simplified to 1/6

hints: How many quarters fit in a half?
practice.explanation: 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = 1/2 × 4/1 = 4/2 = 2. There are 2 quarter-pieces in one half.
